meta.name: Docker Certified Associate (DCA)
meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `docker-dca` tag to 61 questions] [dca batch 1: 18 scenario rewrites]

questions.question: A developer asks 'are an image and a container the same thing?'. The SR engineer explains: ONE is a READ-ONLY artifact built from layered filesystem snapshots (stored in the registry / on disk). The OTHER is a RUNNING (or stopped) INSTANCE of that artifact with its own writable filesystem layer, namespaced PID + network, mounts, etc. Which mapping?
options: Image = read-only layered filesystem template (registry artifact); Container = runtime instance of the image with its own writable layer + namespaces + cgroups
Same thing — false
Image dev / container prod — false; same concepts in any env
Container on disk / image in memory — reversed
questions.explanation: A Docker image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot (read-only). A container is a live, running instance of that image with an additional thin writable layer (copy-on-write). Many containers can share the same underlying image layers, saving disk space. When a container is deleted, its writable layer is lost unless committed or using a volume. a container is a running instance of an image with a writable layer on top

questions.question: A Dockerfile has both `ENTRYPOINT ["python"]` and `CMD ["app.py"]`. The container is run as `docker run myimg main.py`. The user-provided `main.py` REPLACES CMD's default `app.py`. ENTRYPOINT stays. Net result: `python main.py`. Which Dockerfile instruction provides the DEFAULT command that gets OVERRIDDEN by run-args?
options: `CMD` — sets the DEFAULT command (or arguments to ENTRYPOINT); OVERRIDDEN by `docker run image <args>`
`EXEC` — not a Dockerfile instruction
`ENTRYPOINT` — sets the ALWAYS-run executable; only overridden with `--entrypoint`
`RUN` — executes a command DURING image build, not at container start
questions.explanation: CMD sets the default command and/or arguments for a container. It can be completely overridden by providing a command at `docker run`. ENTRYPOINT sets the main executable and is harder to override (requires --entrypoint flag). RUN executes commands during image build. EXEC is not a Dockerfile instruction.

questions.question: An admin starts `nginx` and wants: (a) it runs DETACHED (no terminal attached), (b) it automatically restarts if the container crashes, AND (c) it restarts when the Docker daemon restarts (e.g., after host reboot). Which `docker run` flags?
options: `docker run -d --restart=always nginx` — `-d` detached; `--restart=always` restarts on crash + on daemon restart (host reboot)
`--daemon --always-restart` — not real flags
`--background --restart=on-failure` — `--background` not a flag; `on-failure` only on non-zero exit, not on stop
`-d --keep-alive` — `--keep-alive` not a flag
questions.explanation: -d (detach) runs the container in the background. --restart=always restarts the container regardless of exit code, including after Docker daemon restarts. Other policies: --restart=on-failure (only on non-zero exit), --restart=unless-stopped (always except when manually stopped).

questions.question: An admin wants to PIPE only the container IDs (just the IDs, one per line, no header) to `xargs` for batch operations like `docker rm`. Which `docker ps` invocation prints only IDs?
options: `docker ps -q` — `-q` (`--quiet`) prints only container IDs, one per line; perfect for `xargs`
`docker list --quiet` — `list` is not a verb; it's `ps` or `container ls`
`docker container show --id-only` — `show` is not the right verb
`docker container ls --ids` — `--ids` is not a real flag
questions.explanation: docker ps -q (or docker container ls -q) outputs only container IDs of running containers. Useful for piping: `docker stop $(docker ps -q)` stops all running containers. Add -a to include stopped containers: `docker ps -aq`.

questions.question: A Docker host has built up cruft over time: stopped containers, dangling images (untagged), unused networks, unused build cache. One command CLEANS ALL OF THIS in a single confirmation prompt. Which?
options: `docker clean all` — not a real command
`docker rm --all && docker rmi --all` — `--all` is not a flag; would also require listing
`docker system prune` — removes stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, and unused build cache; `--volumes` also clears unused volumes (separate flag)
`docker purge --system` — not a real command
questions.explanation: `docker system prune` removes all stopped containers, all networks not used by at least one container, all dangling images, and all build cache. Add -a to also remove unused images (not just dangling). Add --volumes to also remove unused volumes. This is the recommended cleanup command.

questions.question: A `Dockerfile` is in a repository alongside `node_modules/` (200 MB), `.git/` (50 MB), `*.log` files. Running `docker build .` sends ALL of those to the Docker daemon (the 'build context'). A file lets you EXCLUDE files from the build context (similar to `.gitignore`). Which?
options: `.dockerignore` — specifies patterns of files / directories to EXCLUDE from the build context sent to the Docker daemon; speeds builds, keeps secrets out, reduces image size
Hidden env vars — different concept (env vars are runtime, not build-context)
Prevent Dockerfile instructions — wrong concept
Block image pulls — wrong concept
questions.explanation: The .dockerignore file works like .gitignore — it tells the Docker CLI which files and directories to exclude when sending the build context to the daemon. This speeds up builds (smaller context), prevents accidentally including secrets (e.g., .env, credentials), and avoids cache-busting from unrelated file changes.

questions.question: A Go service builds with `go build` into a 50 MB statically-linked binary. The build dependencies (go toolchain) are 800 MB. A SINGLE-stage Dockerfile produces an 800 MB image that includes the build toolchain. A MULTI-stage Dockerfile uses multiple FROM instructions: stage 1 builds the binary (uses the toolchain), stage 2 starts FROM scratch and COPYs ONLY the binary. The final image is ~50 MB. Which describes multi-stage builds?
options: Builds multiple images in parallel — false; multiple FROMs in ONE Dockerfile produce ONE final image
Multiple FROM instructions in one Dockerfile separating build + runtime stages; `COPY --from=<stage>` brings artifacts forward; final image excludes build toolchain → MUCH smaller
Multiple OS targets — false; that's `--platform` build flag
Conditional logic — false; multi-stage isn't an if/else feature
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM instructions. Build stages compile/test code with all required build tools. The final stage copies only the compiled artifacts, resulting in a minimal image without compilers, test frameworks, or intermediate files. For example, a Go app: stage 1 uses golang:alpine to compile, stage 2 uses scratch or alpine and copies just the binary — reducing image size from GB to MB. producing a smaller final image without build tools

questions.question: A MySQL container's data must SURVIVE: (a) container restart, (b) container removal, (c) Docker daemon restart, (d) host reboot. The data should live on the host's disk but be MANAGED by Docker (path, lifecycle, permissions). Which mount type?
options: Container writable layer — wiped on container removal; OPPOSITE of persistence
Named Docker volume — managed-by-Docker persistent storage; survives container removal; portable across containers; the canonical persistent storage
tmpfs mount — RAM-backed, lost on container stop
Bind mount to /tmp — host-managed bind mount works for persistence but /tmp is volatile on many distros (cleared at reboot); not the recommended approach
questions.explanation: Named Docker volumes are managed by Docker, portable, easy to back up, and work across different host paths. Bind mounts couple the container to a specific host path, reducing portability. tmpfs mounts are in-memory and lost when the container stops. The container's writable layer is removed with the container. Named volumes are the recommended production storage solution.

questions.question: Two Dockerfile instructions for putting files into an image: `COPY` is straightforward (copies from local context to image). `ADD` does the same BUT ALSO fetches remote URLs AND AUTO-EXTRACTS recognized tar archives (.tar / .tar.gz / .tar.bz2). Best-practice guidance prefers `COPY` unless URL/auto-extract is specifically needed. Which describes the difference?
options: Permissions differ — false; both preserve permissions
Identical / ADD deprecated — false; both supported, but COPY preferred for clarity

`ADD` can fetch HTTP URLs AND auto-extracts tarballs; `COPY` only does local file/directory copy. Best practice: prefer `COPY` for predictability; use `ADD` only when URL fetch or tar auto-extract is genuinely needed
COPY = files only / ADD = directories — false; both handle files and directories
questions.explanation: COPY simply copies files/directories from the build context into the image. ADD additionally: (1) can fetch files from remote URLs, (2) automatically extracts local tar archives (.tar, .tar.gz, etc.) into the destination. Best practice: use COPY by default. Use ADD only when you specifically need URL fetching or tar extraction — its implicit behavior can cause unexpected results. COPY only copies local files/directories — COPY is preferred when you don't need ADD's extra features

questions.question: An ops engineer needs to see EVERYTHING about an image: layer-by-layer history, environment variables, exposed ports, entrypoint + CMD, default user, working directory, labels, config-blob digest. The image's METADATA (not the image content) is what they want. Which command?
options: `docker inspect <image>` — dumps the complete JSON metadata of the image (config + rootfs + history); the canonical inspector
`docker image history <image>` — shows layer-by-layer history but NOT the full config metadata
`docker image info` — not a real command
`docker image describe` — not a real command
questions.explanation: `docker inspect IMAGE` (or `docker image inspect IMAGE`) returns a JSON document with full image metadata: ID, created date, labels, environment variables, exposed ports, entrypoint, cmd, layers, and more. `docker image history` shows the build layers and their sizes. `docker inspect` works on both images and containers.

questions.question: By default, when you `docker run nginx` without specifying a network, the container is attached to the `bridge` network. This is the standard SINGLE-HOST containerised network using a Linux bridge + iptables NAT for outbound and port-publish for inbound. Which network driver provides this single-host NAT-based behaviour?
options: `none` driver — isolates the container with no network at all
`bridge` driver — isolated network on a single host with NAT to host network; default when no `--network` is specified
`overlay` driver — multi-host (Swarm) network; not single-host
`host` driver — shares the host's network namespace; no isolation
questions.explanation: The bridge driver (default for single-host) creates an isolated virtual network. Containers get private IPs and can communicate within the bridge network. Docker performs NAT so containers can reach the internet via the host. The host driver removes network isolation (container shares host's network stack). The overlay driver is for multi-host Swarm networking. none disables networking.

questions.question: Two containers on the SAME custom bridge network `mynet` can connect using `nslookup web` (each other by container name). The SAME two on the DEFAULT bridge network can NOT — name resolution fails. The reason is a fundamental difference between user-defined bridges and the default bridge. Which?
options: The default `bridge` network does NOT have automatic DNS resolution by container name — only USER-DEFINED bridge networks provide built-in DNS-based service discovery between containers
Default bridge is IPv6-only — false
Requires Docker Compose — false; Compose just creates a user-defined network automatically
It does work on default bridge — false
questions.explanation: User-defined bridge networks include an embedded DNS server that resolves container names to their IPs. The default bridge network (docker0) does not have this — containers must use --link (deprecated) or IP addresses to communicate. This is a key reason to always create custom networks: automatic service discovery by name, better isolation, and network-level container grouping.

questions.question: A Docker SWARM has 3 manager + 5 worker nodes. A service deploys 10 replicas across the nodes. The replicas need to communicate as if on the same Layer-2 broadcast domain — but they're on DIFFERENT physical hosts. The Swarm-aware network driver builds an L2 OVERLAY by encapsulating frames in VXLAN. Which driver?
options: `host` driver — direct host networking, no multi-host overlay
`overlay` driver — Swarm multi-host network; encapsulates Ethernet frames in VXLAN (UDP) so containers on different nodes appear on the same L2 broadcast domain
CDN-backed network — wrong concept
Single-node encrypted network — partial; overlay supports encryption (`--opt encrypted=true`), but the defining feature is multi-host
questions.explanation: Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes), enabling containers on different physical/virtual machines to communicate using private IPs. Docker encapsulates traffic in VXLAN packets for host-to-host transport. Overlay networks are the foundation of Swarm service discovery and load balancing. They can be encrypted with --opt encrypted for node-to-node TLS.

questions.question: A Docker host is about to become the FIRST manager of a new Swarm cluster. The admin runs a single command on that host: it generates the join tokens for future manager + worker nodes, initialises the Raft cluster, and the current node becomes the leader. Which command?
options: `docker swarm create --advertise-addr IP` — wrong verb (it's `init`, not `create`)
`docker cluster create --mode manager` — not a real command
`docker swarm start --manager` — not a real verb
`docker swarm init [--advertise-addr <ip>]` — initialises a new Swarm, makes the current node the first manager, generates `swarm join-token manager` and `swarm join-token worker` tokens
questions.explanation: `docker swarm init` initializes a new Swarm and promotes the current node to manager. On machines with multiple network interfaces, add `--advertise-addr IP` to specify the manager's address for other nodes to join. After init, Docker outputs a `docker swarm join --token` command for adding worker nodes.

questions.question: In Docker Swarm: a SERVICE is a DECLARATIVE deployment description — image, replica count, resources, networks, secrets, restart policy. The Swarm scheduler converts that into TASKS — each task is ONE container instance on a node. Tasks are the imperative scheduling unit; services are the desired state. Which describes the difference?
options: A service defines the desired state (image, replicas, resources, networks, secrets); a TASK is one container scheduled by Swarm to a node to satisfy that desired state
Tasks stateless / services state — wrong distinction
Service = 1 container / task = group — reversed
Synonyms — false
questions.explanation: A Swarm service declares desired state: which image to run, how many replicas, resource limits, placement constraints, update policies, etc. The Swarm manager decomposes the service into tasks — each task maps to exactly one container on one node. If a task fails, the manager creates a replacement task to maintain desired replica count. replicas, ports, constraints); a task is the atomic unit of scheduling — one container instance running the service on a specific node

questions.question: A running Swarm service `webapp` currently has 3 replicas. The team wants to scale it to 5. The Swarm scheduler will start 2 more tasks on appropriate nodes. Which command syntax?
options: `docker swarm scale webapp 5` — wrong verb (the scale verb is on `service`, not `swarm`)
`docker service resize webapp --replicas=5` — wrong verb (`resize` not real)
`docker service update webapp --count=5` — wrong flag (`--count` not real; use `--replicas` with `update`)
`docker service scale webapp=5` — the canonical scale syntax for a single service
questions.explanation: `docker service scale webapp=5` sets the replica count for the 'webapp' service to 5. You can scale multiple services at once: `docker service scale webapp=5 api=3`. Alternatively: `docker service update --replicas=5 webapp`. The Swarm manager will schedule new tasks on available nodes or terminate tasks if scaling down.

questions.question: Docker Content Trust (DCT) protects against TAMPERING and IMPERSONATION of images. When DCT is enabled (`DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`), Docker only pulls / runs images whose tag is SIGNED by a trusted publisher. Notary is the signing backend. The signing key chain protects against man-in-the-middle or compromised registry attacks. Which describes DCT?
options: Encrypts at rest in Hub — different concern (data-at-rest, not authenticity)
Requires 2FA — different surface (account auth, not image-trust)
Uses digital signatures (via Notary) to verify images haven't been tampered with since publication — protects against image-tampering / MITM / compromised-registry attacks
Scans for CVEs — that's image vulnerability scanning (different feature, e.g., Snyk / Trivy / Hub scanning)
questions.explanation: Docker Content Trust (DCT) uses The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary to sign and verify images. When enabled (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1), Docker only pulls/runs images with valid signatures. It protects against: man-in-the-middle attacks substituting a legitimate image, running unverified third-party images, and supply chain tampering. Signers use offline root keys and online targets keys.

questions.question: A security-tested container must run with NO NETWORK ACCESS WHATSOEVER — no DNS, no outbound, no inbound. The container should have a loopback interface only. Which Docker network driver?
options: `bridge --icc=false` — disables container-to-container, but the container can still reach external networks
`none` driver — gives the container ONLY a loopback interface; no external networking at all
`isolated` — not a real driver name
`host` driver — exposes ALL host networking; OPPOSITE of no-network
questions.explanation: The 'none' network driver completely disables networking for the container. The container has only a loopback interface. Use it for containers processing local data with no network requirements (batch jobs, file processing), security-sensitive workloads, or containers that should not communicate with anything. `docker run --network=none myimage`.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `docker commit` and why is it generally discouraged?
options: It commits Dockerfile changes to version control; discouraged because it overwrites the original
It creates a new image from a container's current state; discouraged because it creates opaque.
It saves a container's logs to disk; discouraged because logs should use a logging driver
It pushes a local image to a registry; discouraged due to bandwidth costs
questions.explanation: `docker commit CONTAINER IMAGE` snapshots a container's writable layer into a new image. It's discouraged because: (1) the result is a black-box — you can't see what changed, (2) it's not reproducible — others can't build the same image from source, (3) it doesn't work with CI/CD pipelines. Best practice: always define images with Dockerfiles committed to version control. unreproducible images not defined by a Dockerfile

questions.question: What Linux kernel feature does Docker use to limit a container's CPU and memory usage?
options: Linux namespaces
seccomp profiles
SELinux mandatory access controls
Control groups (cgroups)
questions.explanation: Control groups (cgroups) enforce resource limits: CPU shares, CPU quotas, memory limits, block I/O, network bandwidth. For example: `docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 myimage`. Linux namespaces provide isolation (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user namespaces). seccomp limits available syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux enforce MAC policies. Together, these form Docker's container isolation model.

questions.question: Which command lists all volumes on a Docker host, including their names and driver?
options: docker volume list
docker volume ls
docker storage ls
docker volumes show
questions.explanation: `docker volume ls` lists all volumes with their driver and name. To filter: `docker volume ls -f dangling=true` shows volumes not mounted by any container. To remove unused volumes: `docker volume prune`. To inspect a specific volume (including mount point): `docker volume inspect VOLUME_NAME`.

questions.question: In a Dockerfile, what is the effect of running multiple RUN commands versus chaining them with &&?
options: Multiple RUN commands execute in parallel; chaining with && executes sequentially
Each RUN instruction creates a new image layer;.
There is no difference — Docker optimizes them automatically
Chaining with && is only supported in Linux containers
questions.explanation: Each RUN instruction creates a new read-only layer in the image. Multiple RUN commands = multiple layers = larger image. Chaining: `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` produces one layer and keeps the image smaller by cleaning up in the same layer. If you clean in a separate RUN, the cache files still exist in the previous layer. chaining with && keeps them in one layer, reducing image size and layer count

questions.question: What is the purpose of the HEALTHCHECK instruction in a Dockerfile?
options: It validates network connectivity when the container launches
It defines a command Docker runs periodically to test container health.
It validates the Dockerfile syntax during build
It checks if required environment variables are set before the container starts
questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK defines a command that Docker runs at intervals (default: 30s) to determine if the container is functioning correctly. States: starting (initial grace period), healthy (check passes), unhealthy (check fails threshold times). Swarm uses health status to restart unhealthy tasks. Example: `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1`. updating the container's status to healthy, unhealthy, or starting

questions.question: A Swarm service update is in progress and several tasks have become unhealthy. What flag on `docker service update` would automatically pause the update if a task fails?
options: --failure-action=stop
--update-failure-action=pause
--rollback-on-failure=true
--update-policy=halt
questions.explanation: `--update-failure-action=pause` stops the rolling update when a task fails, allowing operators to investigate. Other values: `continue` (default: keep updating even if tasks fail), `rollback` (automatically revert to the previous service spec). Combine with `--update-monitor` (time to observe a task before considering it healthy) and `--update-max-failure-ratio`.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to pass secrets (passwords, API keys) to containers in Docker Swarm?
options: Use Docker Secrets — stored encrypted in the Raft log and only available to authorized services as in-memory tmpfs files
Hardcode secrets in the Docker image
Use environment variables in docker-compose.yml
Mount a host directory containing a secrets file
questions.explanation: Docker Secrets (Swarm only) stores sensitive data encrypted in the Swarm's Raft log. Secrets are decrypted and mounted as in-memory tmpfs files at /run/secrets/SECRET_NAME inside authorized containers — never written to disk. Environment variables are visible in `docker inspect` output and process listings. Hardcoding in images is an obvious anti-pattern. `docker secret create` and `docker service create --secret`.

questions.question: How do you execute an interactive bash shell in a running container named 'myapp'?
options: docker exec -it myapp bash
docker shell myapp
docker attach myapp
docker run -it myapp bash
questions.explanation: `docker exec -it myapp bash` runs a new bash process inside the already-running container. -i (interactive) keeps stdin open; -t allocates a pseudo-TTY. `docker attach` connects your terminal to the container's PID 1 process (not a new shell). `docker run` starts a new container, not inside an existing one.

questions.question: What does the `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` combination achieve when running a container?
options: It prevents the container from becoming root then grants network admin rights
It removes all security profiles then applies the NET_BIND profile
It drops all Linux capabilities then adds back only the ability to bind to ports below 1024,.
It disables networking then re-enables it for specific ports
questions.explanation: Linux capabilities break root privileges into distinct units. `--cap-drop ALL` removes all capabilities from the container. `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` re-adds only the capability to bind to privileged ports (<1024). This follows the principle of least privilege — the container can run a web server on port 80 without any other elevated privileges. Never add SYS_ADMIN unless absolutely necessary. following the principle of least privilege

questions.question: What is a Docker registry and how does it differ from Docker Hub?
options: A registry is the server-side storage and distribution system for Docker images;.
A Docker registry is the same as Docker Hub — they are synonymous
Docker Hub is an open-source project; a registry is Docker's commercial product
A registry stores container logs; Docker Hub stores images
questions.explanation: A Docker registry is any service that stores and serves Docker images using the Docker Registry HTTP API V2. Docker Hub is Docker's public hosted registry. Organizations run private registries for security/performance: Docker Trusted Registry (DTR, enterprise), Harbor, AWS ECR, GCR, Azure ACR. The registry is the infrastructure; Docker Hub is one implementation of it. Docker Hub is a specific public registry hosted by Docker Inc.

questions.question: You want to tag an existing image 'myapp:latest' for pushing to a private registry at 'registry.company.com'. What is the correct command sequence?
options: docker rename myapp:latest registry.company.com/myapp:latest && docker upload
docker tag myapp:latest registry.company.com/myapp:latest && docker push registry.company.com/myapp:latest
docker image publish myapp:latest --registry registry.company.com
docker push registry.company.com/myapp:latest
questions.explanation: Docker images must be tagged with the registry hostname before pushing. `docker tag SOURCE DESTINATION` creates an alias pointing to the same image ID. Then `docker push DESTINATION` uploads all layers to the registry. You must be authenticated (`docker login registry.company.com`) before pushing. The format is: [registry/][repository/]name[:tag].

questions.question: What is the difference between a bind mount and a Docker volume?
options: Volumes support only read-only access; bind mounts support read-write
Bind mounts work on Linux only; volumes work on all platforms
Bind mounts map a specific host path into the container;.
Bind mounts are faster; volumes are more portable
questions.explanation: Bind mounts: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path` — tightly couples the container to a specific host directory. Great for development (live code editing) but reduces portability. Docker volumes: `docker run -v myvolume:/container/path` — Docker manages the storage location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), independent lifecycle, easier to backup/migrate, work with volume drivers for cloud storage (EBS, NFS, etc.). Docker volumes are managed by Docker with their own lifecycle independent of containers

questions.question: How does Docker image layer caching work during builds, and what action breaks the cache for subsequent instructions?
options: Docker caches the entire image; any change rebuilds everything from scratch
Docker caches only RUN instructions; COPY and ADD always rebuild
Docker caches each layer;.
Cache is based on the image tag; changing the tag forces a full rebuild
questions.explanation: Docker checks the cache by comparing each instruction and its context. If a COPY instruction's source files changed, that layer and all layers below it are rebuilt. Key optimization: put frequently changing instructions (COPY source code) AFTER infrequently changing ones (RUN apt-get install). This way, dependency installation is cached even when source code changes. `docker build --no-cache` bypasses all caching. a cache miss for any instruction (changed instruction or changed files it copies) invalidates the cache for that instruction AND all subsequent instructions

questions.question: In Docker Swarm, what is a 'global' service mode and when would you use it?
options: A service shared between multiple Swarms in a federated setup
A service that runs exactly one task on every node in the Swarm.
A service accessible from outside the Swarm via a public IP
A service with unlimited replicas that scales across all nodes
questions.explanation: Global mode services run exactly one task per node (similar to Kubernetes DaemonSets). As nodes join the Swarm, tasks are automatically scheduled on them. As nodes leave, tasks are cleaned up. Perfect for: node-level monitoring agents (Prometheus Node Exporter), log shippers (Fluentd), security scanners, or any workload that must run on every node. Create with: `docker service create --mode=global IMAGE`. used for monitoring agents, log shippers, and security scanners

questions.question: What does the `docker save` command do and how does it differ from `docker export`?
options: docker save saves to a registry; docker export saves to the local filesystem
They are identical — both save a container's data
docker save saves running container state; docker export saves image layers
docker save exports an image with all its layers and metadata to a tar archive;.
questions.explanation: `docker save IMAGE > image.tar` preserves the complete image: all layers, tags, and metadata. Use to transfer images without a registry. `docker export CONTAINER > container.tar` saves the container's flat filesystem only — no layers, no history. `docker save` → `docker load` preserves the image with layers. `docker export` → `docker import` creates a single-layer image. Use save/load for images, export/import for container snapshots. docker export exports a container's filesystem without image metadata or history

questions.question: A production container is crashing repeatedly. Which command shows the container's STDOUT/STDERR output for debugging?
options: docker container stdout CONTAINER
docker inspect CONTAINER --logs
docker debug CONTAINER
docker logs CONTAINER
questions.explanation: `docker logs CONTAINER` shows the container's stdout/stderr history. Useful flags: -f (follow, like tail -f), --tail N (last N lines), --since TIMESTAMP (since a specific time), --timestamps. For production, use a logging driver (json-file, syslog, fluentd, splunk, gelf) to forward logs to a centralized system. Check logs even for stopped containers (unless --rm was used).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the USER instruction in a Dockerfile?
options: It sets the user (and optionally group) that subsequent RUN.
It restricts which users can execute docker run on the image
It defines which users can pull the image from a registry
It creates a new system user account on the host when the container starts
questions.explanation: By default, containers run as root (UID 0), which is a security risk — a container escape would give the attacker root on the host. The USER instruction sets a non-root user for subsequent instructions and the final container. Best practice: create a dedicated user (RUN useradd -r appuser) then set USER appuser before CMD/ENTRYPOINT. Rootless containers reduce the blast radius of vulnerabilities. CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions run as — critical for avoiding running as root

questions.question: Which Docker network command connects an already-running container to an additional network?
options: docker container network-add CONTAINER NETWORK
docker run --network=NETWORK CONTAINER (must be set at run time)
docker network connect NETWORK CONTAINER
docker network join NETWORK CONTAINER
questions.explanation: `docker network connect NETWORK CONTAINER` attaches a running container to an additional network. The container immediately gets an IP address on that network. This is useful for connecting containers to multiple networks (e.g., a frontend network and a backend network). The reverse: `docker network disconnect NETWORK CONTAINER`.

questions.question: What is the role of a Swarm manager node and what happens if a majority of managers become unavailable?
options: Losing any manager immediately stops all running containers in the Swarm
Worker nodes automatically promote themselves to managers if all managers fail
Managers run application workloads only; losing managers doesn't affect running services
Managers use the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain cluster state;.
questions.explanation: Swarm managers use Raft consensus to maintain a consistent distributed state store. For a cluster of N managers, quorum requires (N/2)+1 managers available. With quorum lost, the Swarm enters a read-only state — running containers continue, but no new services can be created, scaled, or updated. Recommendation: use 3 or 5 managers (tolerates 1 or 2 failures). Never use even numbers of managers. losing quorum (majority of managers) prevents scheduling changes — existing tasks continue but no new tasks can be scheduled

questions.question: What is a tmpfs mount in Docker and when is it appropriate?
options: A compressed filesystem that Docker uses to reduce layer sizes
A read-only filesystem for sharing static assets between containers
An in-memory filesystem mounted inside a container.
A temporary filesystem on disk used for container build caches
questions.explanation: tmpfs mounts are stored in the host's memory only (never on disk). Data is temporary — lost when the container stops or restarts. Use cases: storing session tokens, credentials, or other sensitive data that should never touch disk; high-performance temporary scratch space. `docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m myimage`. Available only on Linux. For secrets: use Docker Secrets in Swarm instead. data is never written to disk and is lost when the container stops; ideal for sensitive temporary data

questions.question: You need to limit a container to use at most 256 MB of memory and 0.5 CPUs. What are the correct flags?
options: --memory=256m --cpus=0.5
--mem-limit=256mb --cpu-quota=50
--ram=256M --cpu=half
--memory=256 --cpu-shares=0.5
questions.explanation: --memory=256m sets a hard memory limit (container OOM-killed if exceeded). --cpus=0.5 limits to half a CPU (equivalent to --cpu-quota=50000 --cpu-period=100000). Other useful flags: --memory-swap (total memory+swap limit), --cpu-shares (relative weight, soft limit), --oom-kill-disable (don't OOM kill, but risky). Always set memory limits in production to prevent one container starving others.

questions.question: What does `docker image prune -a` do?
options: Removes all images older than 24 hours
Removes dangling images (untagged, not referenced by any container) only
Removes all unused images (not referenced by any container).
Removes all images including those currently used by running containers
questions.explanation: `docker image prune` (without -a) only removes dangling images — untagged layers with no name. `-a` (--all) removes all images not currently used by at least one container (running or stopped). This reclaims significant disk space on CI/CD servers. Use `--filter` to narrow scope: `docker image prune -a --filter until=24h` removes images older than 24 hours. including tagged images not just dangling ones

questions.question: In Docker Compose, what does the `depends_on` key control?
options: It ensures the dependent service is healthy before starting the dependent container
It creates a network link between the services for name resolution
It copies configuration from one service to another
It controls startup order only.
questions.explanation: `depends_on` controls startup and shutdown ORDER — it does not wait for a service to be 'ready'. For example, a web app with `depends_on: [db]` will start AFTER the db container starts, but not after PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections. For readiness: use `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` combined with a HEALTHCHECK, or implement retry logic in the application. Docker starts services in dependency order, but does not wait for a service to be ready/healthy

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `EXPOSE` instruction in a Dockerfile?
options: It configures the firewall to allow traffic on the specified port
It opens the specified port on the host and maps it to the container
It documents which ports the container application listens on.
It exposes environment variables to external processes
questions.explanation: EXPOSE is documentation — it tells users and orchestration systems which ports the container application intends to listen on. It does NOT publish the port to the host. To actually publish: `docker run -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT` (explicit) or `docker run -P` (auto-publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports). Kubernetes and Swarm use EXPOSE metadata for service mesh configuration. does not actually publish ports to the host

questions.question: What Linux kernel feature provides process, network, mount, and user isolation for containers?
options: Control groups (cgroups)
AppArmor
seccomp
Linux namespaces
questions.explanation: Linux namespaces provide isolation at the kernel level. Docker uses: PID namespace (isolated process tree), Network namespace (isolated network stack, interfaces), Mount namespace (isolated filesystem), UTS namespace (isolated hostname), IPC namespace (isolated shared memory), User namespace (map container root to unprivileged host UID). Cgroups limit resources. seccomp limits syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux enforce access control policies.

questions.question: A service in Docker Swarm needs access to configuration that varies between environments (dev/staging/prod). What is the best approach?
options: Use bind mounts from a shared NFS volume
Use environment variables in the Dockerfile
Use Docker Configs to store non-sensitive configuration data in the Swarm and mount it into services
Build separate images per environment with configurations baked in
questions.explanation: Docker Configs (introduced in Docker 17.06) store non-sensitive configuration files in the Swarm's Raft log and mount them into containers at a specified path (similar to Secrets but for non-sensitive data). `docker config create nginx.conf nginx.conf` then `docker service create --config source=nginx.conf,target=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf nginx`. Configs are immutable; update by creating a new config version.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `--read-only` flag when running a container?
options: It mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only.
It makes the Docker image read-only so it cannot be tagged or modified
It prevents other containers from reading this container's files
It makes the container's configuration immutable
questions.explanation: `docker run --read-only myimage` mounts the container's root filesystem read-only. Any attempt to write to the container filesystem fails. This is a strong security control: (1) prevents malware from writing persistence mechanisms, (2) ensures all state is explicitly in volumes, (3) makes container behavior more predictable. Combine with `--tmpfs /tmp` for applications that need a temporary writable area. preventing any writes to the container layer — improves security and forces explicit volume usage for writable data

questions.question: How do you view real-time resource usage (CPU, memory, network I/O) for all running containers?
options: docker container metrics
docker top --all
docker stats
docker inspect --stats
questions.explanation: `docker stats` shows a live-updating stream of resource metrics for all running containers: CPU%, memory usage/limit, net I/O, block I/O, PIDs. Specify a container name/ID to watch a single container: `docker stats mycontainer`. Add --no-stream for a one-shot snapshot (useful in scripts). `docker top CONTAINER` shows the processes running inside a specific container.

questions.question: Which Dockerfile instruction is used to set environment variables that are available both at build time and at runtime?
options: ARG
VARIABLE
SET
ENV
questions.explanation: ENV sets environment variables that persist in the image and are available to the container at runtime. `ENV NODE_ENV=production`. ARG defines build-time variables (only available during docker build, not in the running container). ARGs are useful for version numbers, build IDs. ENVs are for runtime configuration. Note: ENV variables are visible in `docker inspect` output — don't use for secrets.

questions.question: You need to copy a file from a running container to your local machine. What is the correct command?
options: docker transfer CONTAINER:/path ./local/
docker pull CONTAINER:/path/to/file ./local/
docker export CONTAINER --file /path/to/file
docker cp CONTAINER:/path/to/file ./local/
questions.explanation: `docker cp SOURCE DEST` copies files between a container and the local filesystem. Container paths are specified as `CONTAINER:/path`. Examples: `docker cp myapp:/app/logs/error.log .` copies from container to current directory. `docker cp ./config.json myapp:/app/config.json` copies from host to container. Works on both running and stopped containers.

questions.question: What does an ENTRYPOINT in exec form vs shell form mean in a Dockerfile?
options: They behave identically — the distinction is only syntactic
Exec form uses JSON array syntax and runs directly as PID 1 without a shell;.
Shell form is newer and preferred; exec form is deprecated
Exec form requires the command to be in the PATH; shell form allows full bash scripting
questions.explanation: Exec form: `ENTRYPOINT ["executable", "arg1"]` — runs directly as PID 1. Signals (SIGTERM, SIGINT) are received directly by the process, enabling graceful shutdown. Shell form: `ENTRYPOINT command arg1` — runs as `/bin/sh -c 'command arg1'`. The shell becomes PID 1 and may not forward signals to the actual process. Best practice: use exec form for ENTRYPOINT and CMD to ensure proper signal handling. shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh -c, meaning signals may not be properly forwarded

questions.question: In Docker Swarm, what is an ingress network and what role does it play?
options: The default overlay network that enables routing mesh.
A private network connecting manager nodes for Raft consensus traffic
A monitoring network for collecting container metrics
A network dedicated to external load balancer communication
questions.explanation: The ingress network (created automatically with `docker swarm init`) enables the Swarm routing mesh. When a service publishes port 8080, EVERY Swarm node listens on port 8080. Traffic arriving on any node is load-balanced to a healthy task, regardless of which node the task runs on. This means you can point a load balancer at any node IP. Created as an overlay network with IPVS-based load balancing. allowing any Swarm node to receive traffic for a published service port and route it to a healthy task, regardless of which node runs the task

questions.question: Which command shows the history of image layers, including the size contribution of each layer?
options: docker layer list IMAGE
docker image inspect IMAGE --layers
docker image layers IMAGE --verbose
docker image history IMAGE
questions.explanation: `docker image history IMAGE` lists all layers with their creating command, creation date, and size. Useful for: identifying large layers (targets for optimization), understanding what each layer does, debugging unexpected image sizes. The `<missing>` entries are normal for intermediate stages in multi-stage builds or when the parent image was built elsewhere.

questions.question: What happens to a Docker Swarm service's tasks when you drain a node?
options: All tasks on that node are terminated and not rescheduled
The node is removed from the Swarm permanently
Tasks continue running but new tasks cannot start on that node
The node is marked Drain availability;.
questions.explanation: `docker node update --availability=drain NODE` marks the node as unavailable for new tasks and evicts existing tasks. The Swarm scheduler places replacement tasks on Active nodes. Use before maintenance (patching, rebooting) to gracefully move workloads. After maintenance: `docker node update --availability=active NODE` to return it to the pool. The node remains in the Swarm — only its availability changes. the Swarm scheduler stops placing new tasks on it and reschedules existing tasks to other available nodes

questions.question: What is a seccomp profile in Docker and what does it limit?
options: It encrypts inter-container communication
It restricts which Linux system calls (syscalls) a container process can make, reducing the kernel attack surface
It controls which Docker commands users can run
It limits network bandwidth for the container
questions.explanation: seccomp (secure computing mode) is a Linux kernel feature that filters syscalls. Docker applies a default seccomp profile blocking ~44 dangerous syscalls (e.g., keyctl, add_key, reboot). Custom profiles allow you to restrict further (whitelist-based) or allow more (for specific use cases). To disable: `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (not recommended). Combined with namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, and AppArmor/SELinux for defense-in-depth.

questions.question: How do you update a running Swarm service to use a new image version with zero downtime?
options: docker service restart SERVICE --image NEW_IMAGE
docker service update --image NEW_IMAGE:VERSION SERVICE
docker service redeploy SERVICE --tag NEW_TAG
docker swarm update --service SERVICE --image NEW_IMAGE
questions.explanation: `docker service update --image NEW_IMAGE:VERSION SERVICE` triggers a rolling update. Docker replaces tasks one by one (or in parallel batches based on --update-parallelism), waits for new tasks to start and pass health checks before proceeding. Configure update behavior: --update-parallelism (tasks updated simultaneously), --update-delay (time between batches), --update-failure-action (pause/continue/rollback on failure).

questions.question: What is Docker BuildKit and what improvements does it bring over the classic builder?
options: BuildKit replaces Docker Compose for local development builds
BuildKit adds support for Windows containers only
BuildKit is Docker's commercial add-on for enterprise builds
BuildKit is Docker's modern build subsystem offering parallel build steps.
questions.explanation: BuildKit (enabled with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 or default in recent Docker versions) brings: concurrent layer building (faster multi-stage builds), intelligent cache management, `RUN --mount=type=secret` (secrets available at build time but NOT stored in the image), `RUN --mount=type=ssh` (SSH agent forwarding for private repos), better progress output, and inline cache. Use `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` at the top of your Dockerfile to enable all features. improved caching, secret mounts (never stored in layers), SSH forwarding, and smaller build contexts

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `WORKDIR` instruction in a Dockerfile?
options: It sets the working directory for subsequent RUN.
It specifies the working directory on the host machine during builds
It defines where Docker stores image layers on the host
It mounts a host directory into the container at build time
questions.explanation: WORKDIR sets the current directory context for all subsequent instructions and for the container's shell when running interactively. It creates the directory if it doesn't exist. Best practice: always set WORKDIR instead of `RUN cd /app`. Multiple WORKDIR instructions accumulate: WORKDIR /app followed by WORKDIR src resolves to /app/src. Use absolute paths for clarity. CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, and ADD instructions — creating the directory if it doesn't exist

questions.question: Which Docker plugin type allows you to use cloud storage backends (S3, EBS, Azure Disk) as Docker volumes?
options: Authorization plugins
Volume plugins (volume drivers)
Logging plugins
Network plugins
questions.explanation: Volume plugins (volume drivers) extend Docker's storage capabilities beyond the local filesystem. Popular drivers: REX-Ray (multi-cloud: AWS EBS, S3, Azure Disk, GCE PD), Portworx (cloud-native distributed storage), NFS driver, local-persist. Install a driver, then: `docker volume create --driver rexray/ebs --name myvol`. Swarm services can use volume drivers for persistent storage across nodes.

questions.question: You need to pass a build-time variable (e.g., app version) to a Docker build without embedding it permanently in the image. Which instruction should you use?
options: ENV VERSION=1.0
ARG VERSION
BUILD_ARG VERSION
PARAM VERSION
questions.explanation: ARG defines a build-time variable: `ARG VERSION` in the Dockerfile, then `docker build --build-arg VERSION=2.1.0 .`. ARG values are NOT persisted in the final image (unlike ENV). Use for: version numbers, build metadata, registry URLs. Important: ARG values are visible in `docker history` — don't use for secrets. For secrets at build time: use BuildKit's `RUN --mount=type=secret`.

questions.question: What does the `docker network inspect NETWORK` command return?
options: A summary of firewall rules applied to the network
Real-time traffic statistics for the network
The network's DNS configuration and resolver settings only
A JSON document with network metadata: driver.
questions.explanation: `docker network inspect NETWORK` returns JSON with: network ID, name, driver, scope, subnet/gateway, labels, options, and Containers — a map of connected containers with their IPs on that network. Invaluable for debugging connectivity issues: confirming a container is attached, verifying IP addresses, checking subnet overlap. Works on all network types (bridge, overlay, macvlan). subnet, gateway, options, and a list of connected containers with their IPs

questions.question: What is the minimal recommended Swarm manager configuration for a production cluster that tolerates one manager failure?
options: 2 managers
5 managers
3 managers
1 manager (single manager is sufficient for small clusters)
questions.explanation: With 3 managers, the Raft quorum requires 2 (majority). Tolerates 1 manager failure. Formula: tolerate F failures → need 2F+1 managers. So: 3 managers = tolerate 1, 5 managers = tolerate 2, 7 managers = tolerate 3. Never use 2 managers (quorum = 2, provides no fault tolerance — worse than 1 manager). Recommended: 3 for small/medium production, 5 for critical clusters. Keep managers on separate nodes/racks/AZs.

questions.question: Which TWO Dockerfile instructions create a new image LAYER?
options: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
COPY ./app /opt/app
EXPOSE 8080
WORKDIR /opt/app
questions.explanation: RUN and COPY (and ADD) create new filesystem layers. EXPOSE and WORKDIR (along with ENV, LABEL, USER, ARG, CMD, ENTRYPOINT) only add metadata to the image; they don't produce a content layer. Modern BuildKit may collapse some, but conceptually only filesystem-modifying instructions are layers.
